blocks.text: [II, 839] The former, namely רננים renanim, could, while the vowels were absent, be read ronenim, that is, singing, praising, exulting, etc. Hence arose those versions, wing of the praising, wing of the rejoicing, etc., in the Elders, Aquila and others. But the Chaldee and Jerome, even though the points were lacking, nevertheless rightly gathered from the sequence of the words that רננים is something else, namely the name of a bird. And all the Hebrews embrace the same opinion, although they cannot determine which birds are called רננים renanim. The Chaldee renders it cock, not the common one, but תרנגול דמשבחא ומקלסא, the cock which praises and celebrates God. Of which the same translator speaks on the words of Job cursing his day, Iob. III, 7. Let no song come into it: לא תעול רננא דתרנגול ברא למקלסה בה, Let not the song of the wild cock come to praise in it. And on Iobi XXXVIII, 36. מי שוי בכלין חוכמתא או יהב לתרנגול ברא בינתא למקלסה למריה, Who has put wisdom in the reins? or given the wild cock understanding to praise his Lord? And on Psal. L, 11. גלין קדמי כל מיני עופא דפרחין באויר שמיא ותרנגול ברא דקרסולי שרין בארעא ורישיה מטי בשמיא מרנן קדמי, Known to me are all the kinds of birds that fly in the air of the heavens; and the wild cock, whose feet stand on the earth and whose head reaches to heaven, sings before me. Of this same cock Mahomet speaks thus in the Chronica Espahan: لله ديك ابيض جناحاه موشيا بالزبرجد والياقوت واللولو له جناح بالمشرق وجناح بالمغرب وراسه تحت العرش وقوايمه في الهوي يوذن في كل سحر فيسمع اهل السموات والارض الا الثقلين الجن والانس فعند ذلك تجيبه ديوك الارض فاذا دنا يوم القيمة يقال الله تعالي له ضم جناحيك وغض صوتك فيعلم اهل السموات والارض الا الثقلين ان الساعة قد اقتربت [li-llāh dīk abyaḍ janāḥāhu mawshiyyā bi-l-zabarjad wa-l-yāqūt wa-l-luʾluʾ lahu janāḥ bi-l-mashriq wa-janāḥ bi-l-maghrib wa-raʾsuhu taḥt al-ʿarsh wa-qawāʾimuhu fī al-hawā yuʾadhdhin fī kull saḥar fa-yasmaʿ ahl al-samawāt wa-l-arḍ illā al-thaqalayn al-jinn wa-l-ins fa-ʿinda dhālika tujībuhu duyūk al-arḍ fa-idhā danā yawm al-qiyāma yaqūl Allāh taʿālā lahu ḍumma janāḥayka wa-ghuḍḍ ṣawtaka fa-yaʿlam ahl al-samawāt wa-l-arḍ illā al-thaqalayn anna al-sāʿa qad iqtarabat] God has a white cock, whose wings are adorned with emeralds, carbuncles and pearls. One of them is spread towards the east, the other towards the west; its head is beneath the throne of glory, and its feet in the air. Every morning it calls to prayer, and all the inhabitants of heaven and earth hear it, except men and [col. 240] demons. Therefore the cocks of the earth answer it. And when the day of judgement is at hand, God Most High will say to it: Draw in your wings and restrain your voice, so that all the inhabitants of heaven and earth, except men and demons, may know that the hour is at hand. Because this fabulous cock is imagined to praise God at fixed hours, whence it is called מרנן merannen, praising, Psal. L, 11., and its song רננא renana, Iob. III, 7., the circumcised doctors would have the same cock signified by the word רננים renanim in the passage with which we are dealing. But it is strange that that cock should be called by a plural word, since it is unique. The same objection could be raised against R. Selomo. For to him רננים renanim is that bird which in the [II, 840] Mishnah is called בר יוכני bor juchne, or son of the nest, of which we spoke above ^{a)}; and it too is singular and unique in its kind.

But, bidding farewell to these trifles, let us hear others. R. Levi doubts whether both words, כנף רננים canaph renanim, or only the latter, belong to the name of this bird. Aben Ezra holds that it is called renanim from the verb רנן ranan, which means to sing, בעבור נועם קולו, on account of the elegance of its voice. And in Pomarius some declare it to be a bird שמתפאר בקולו הערב רוסיניולו בלעז, which displays the sweetness of its voice, called in Italian rossignuolo, that is, nightingale. Yet he himself prefers the peacock to be understood, שמתפאר בראיית כנפיו, which glories in the display of its feathers. And between the two opinions Kimchi is so undecided that he leans rather to the latter. Perhaps, he says, it is a songbird, and so called from the modulation of its song: או מרנן ומתעלס בכנפיו שהם יפות כמו הטווס ואולי הוא הוא, or it is a bird which rejoices and exults because of the beauty of its feathers, like the peacock, and perhaps it is the peacock itself. This opinion, although new and put forward only hesitantly, has nevertheless been received by our scholars with the greatest applause, as being truer than what happened at the Sagra [the proverb for a thing beyond doubt]. Thus Pagninus here has The peacock exults in its wings. So also Mercerus. And Junius, the wing of peacocks is to be exulted in. And all the vernacular versions in all languages that I have been able to come across follow the same. For all who have known the peacock, whether from books or from αὐτοψίᾳ [autopsia], know that it displays its feathers with pomp and pride, and so exults and prides itself in their beauty. Hence Ovid in book 1 of the Art [of Love]:
The bird of Juno displays its feathers when praised: If you watch in silence, it hides away its riches.
The bird of Juno spreads before man its praised feathers, and the bird is very proud of its beauty.
